faq.a: It penetrates anaerobic tissues, is inexpensive, and its DNA‑damage mechanism works against all obligate anaerobes.
faq.q: Why is metronidazole preferred for most anaerobic infections?

faq.a: It often shows few organisms despite many leukocytes; a negative stain does not rule out anaerobic infection.
faq.q: Can a Gram stain reliably detect anaerobes?

faq.a: Rely on clinical picture, imaging, and start empiric metronidazole; obtain any available pus for Gram stain.
faq.q: What if anaerobic culture facilities are absent?

exam: A 45‑year‑old alcoholic presents with foul‑smelling sputum and a cavitary lesion on CXR – what is the most likely organism and initial therapy? — Bacteroides spp.; start metronidazole and arrange chest drainage.
A diabetic patient has rapidly spreading thigh swelling with gas on ultrasound; what is the next urgent step? — Immediate surgical debridement and start metronidazole plus broad‑spectrum coverage.
In a resource‑limited hospital, you cannot obtain an anaerobic culture; how do you confirm the diagnosis? — Use clinical risk factors, imaging, and Gram stain; begin empiric metronidazole.
Why is clindamycin used for necrotizing fasciitis caused by anaerobes despite higher cost? — It suppresses toxin production and covers both anaerobes and some streptococci.
A patient on metronidazole develops peripheral neuropathy; what alternative regimen can you use? — Switch to clindamycin or a β‑lactam/β‑lactamase inhibitor if no contraindications.
How does HIV infection increase the risk of anaerobic lung abscess? — Impaired mucosal immunity leads to aspiration of oral anaerobes and reduced clearance.
What imaging finding distinguishes an empyema from a simple pleural effusion? — Loculated fluid with split pleura sign on CT; requires drainage.
ai.title: Anaerobic Bacterial Infections
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Anaerobic bacteria cause deep‑seated infections, especially in low‑resource settings where oral hygiene, trauma, and HIV are common. Diagnosis relies on clinical clues and limited lab tests; metronidazole remains first‑line therapy.

b: Common genera: Bacteroides, Prevotella, Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Clostridium.
Account for 20‑30% of intra‑abdominal infections and >50% of necrotizing soft‑tissue infections in tropical hospitals.
sections.p: Anaerobic bacteria thrive without oxygen and are part of normal flora of the mouth, gut, and female genital tract. When mucosal barriers are breached they cause polymicrobial infections that progress rapidly.

b: Gram‑negative rods (Bacteroides, Prevotella) are non‑spore‑forming; Gram‑positive cocci (Peptostreptococcus) are spore‑negative.
Produce foul‑smelling, gray‑white pus; gas may be present in deep tissues.
sections.p: Obligate anaerobes lack cytochrome oxidase and produce enzymes (e.g., collagenases, β‑lactamases) that facilitate tissue destruction and antibiotic resistance.

b: Oral cavity → lung abscess after aspiration.
Genital tract → bacterial vaginosis, postpartum endometritis.
sections.p: Infection follows endogenous spread after mucosal disruption (tooth extraction, childbirth, bowel perforation) or exogenous inoculation (trauma, contaminated dressings).

b: Lung abscess and empyema (aspiration in alcoholics, HIV).
Necrotizing fasciitis and Fournier’s gangrene (trauma, diabetes).
Intra‑abdominal abscess, peritonitis, and pelvic sepsis (appendicitis, perforated ulcer, obstetric procedures).
Brain abscess after otitis media or sinusitis.
sections.p: Anaerobes produce a spectrum of deep infections that are often polymicrobial and present with subtle early signs.
Clinical suspicion is paramount; laboratory support is limited in low‑resource settings.

t.b: Is the organism Gram‑negative rod or Gram‑positive cocci? Presence of many leukocytes with few organisms suggests anaerobes.
Confirms species; growth only in anaerobic chamber indicates obligate anaerobe.
Detects abscess cavity, gas formation, or empyema; guides drainage.
Identifies fluid collections when CT unavailable; guides bedside aspiration.

b: Combination β‑lactam/β‑lactamase inhibitor (e.g., ampicillin‑sulbactam) when mixed aerobic‑anaerobic flora expected.
Avoid monotherapy with cephalosporins lacking β‑lactamase stability (e.g., ceftriaxone) as many Bacteroides produce β‑lactamases.
sections.p: Prompt antimicrobial therapy plus source control (drainage, debridement) reduces mortality.

t.b: What is the definitive source control? Removes pus, reduces bacterial load, and provides material for culture.
Is the collection resolving? Persistent cavity suggests need for further drainage or change of antibiotics.

b: Key history: recent dental work, alcohol use, HIV, obstetric procedures, trauma.
Physical clue: foul‑smelling discharge or gas‑filled swelling.
Urgent step: start metronidazole and arrange drainage before culture results return.
sections.p: Focus on clinical pattern, risk factors, and pragmatic management steps.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly expanding soft‑tissue swelling with systemic toxicity (fever >38 °C, tachycardia, hypotension).
New‑onset respiratory distress from lung abscess or empyema.
